newsitem.title: HONG KONG: China Grain - Domestic soymeal seen heading lower.
newsitem.headline: China Grain - Domestic soymeal seen heading lower.

text.p: A sharp increase in soymeal arrivals at Chinese ports could depress domestic meal prices towards 2,550 yuan ($307) a tonne over the next two months from about 2,750 yuan now, Hong Kong-based traders said on Thursday.
"The meal price may keep going down, possibly as low as 2,550 yuan per tonne," said a Beijing-based trader.
Estimates of arrival volumes varied from 500,000 to 600,000 tonnes of soymeal expected during the entire month of January.
"We have another (meal) vessel in India and we don't know how to handle it," said one trader.
Shanghai sources said on Wednesday about one million tonnes of soymeal were clogging Chinese ports.
But a Chinese trader said at least another 400,000 tonnes of meal were expected to arrive between now and July.
About 450,000 tonnes of soybeans were also expected to land at China's gates in January, a senior trader estimated.
The huge Chinese import bottleneck has pressured U.S. soy futures, but the price falls have not attracted buyers who are concerned they may be left with moulding stocks.
"That stuff (soymeal) gets mouldy very quickly," a grains trader said, noting that China's interest in fresh deals of meal and beans remained non-existent and the market was saturated.
One trader said he had switched from selling soymeal to selling cotton as the prospects there were brighter.
Asian traders reported a number of recent corn deals in the region in packages of 12,000 tonnes.
Chinese origin corn was reported done at $143 a tonne C&F for prompt shipment and export prices ex-Dalian wwere quoted at about 1,040 yuan ($125) a tonne, they said.

U.S. origin corn was heard done for March shipment at $139.90 a tonne, with seller's option for U.S. or Argentine origin for early March shipment at $137.20 a tonne and seller's option for U.S., Argentine or Chinese at $134.20 a tonne C&F.
Traders said price indications for soybeans and meal to China were simply theoretical, since the market saw very few enquiries and interest was comatose.
Indian meal was particularly high-priced at the moment as the crushing season was nearing its end, sources said.
